```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

D <- "data/derived/"
rd <- function(f) read_csv(paste0(D, f), show_col_types = FALSE)

game      <- rd("game_results.csv")
gs        <- rd("game_stats.csv")
gbench    <- rd("game_benchmarks.csv")
sens      <- rd("run_date_sensitivity.csv")
orig      <- rd("original_metrics.csv")
strat     <- rd("strategy_returns.csv")
summ      <- rd("strategy_summary.csv")
ics       <- rd("ic_summary.csv")
seeds     <- rd("seed_robustness.csv")
reco      <- rd("game_recommendation.csv")

pct  <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
num  <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
gb   <- function(name) gbench$return[str_detect(gbench$portfolio, name)]
ic   <- function(m) ics |> filter(model == m)
s    <- function(st) summ |> filter(strategy == st)
```

In class, 45 teams each ran two $100,000 portfolios from 26 August to 1 November 2026. One
was picked by intuition; the other followed a gradient boosting model. This post asks:
**did the model actually predict which stocks would outperform, and can a better-built
version do it?**

## The experiment

The class model is XGBoost on 95 large US stocks. From daily prices it builds momentum over
one, three and six months, one-month volatility, five-day reversal and the day's return
relative to SPY, and predicts each stock's return over the next 20 trading days. It trains
on 2022-2023, tests on 2024 onward, and each month buys the ten stocks with the highest
forecasts. Its backtest printed a Sharpe ratio of `r num(orig$sharpe_as_coded, 1)`.

## What we learned from the game

Model portfolios returned `r pct(gs$mean_model)` on average against
`r pct(gs$mean_intuition)` for intuition, and won for `r round(100 * gs$share_model_better)`
percent of teams. That is weaker evidence than it looks: the paired test gives
p = `r num(gs$p_paired)`, and the bootstrap 95 percent interval for the gap runs from
`r pct(gs$boot_lo)` to `r pct(gs$boot_hi)`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-game
#| fig-cap: "Returns of the 45 teams' portfolios over the game. Reference lines: SPY, the 95 stocks held equally, and the class code's recommendation rerun on 26 August and held to the end."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4
refs <- tibble(y = c(gb("^SPY"), gb("equal-weight"), gb("model recommendation")),
               label = c("SPY", "95 stocks, equal weight", "code rerun on 26 Aug"))

game |>
  pivot_longer(c(intuition, model), names_to = "portfolio", values_to = "ret") |>
  mutate(portfolio = recode(portfolio, intuition = "intuition", model = "model-based")) |>
  ggplot(aes(portfolio, ret)) +
  geom_hline(data = refs, aes(yintercept = y, linetype = label), colour = "grey35") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.35, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8, colour = "#0072B2") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dotted", "dashed", "solid"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "return over the game") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

Rerunning the posted code on the game's first morning, its ten picks lost
`r pct(-gb("model recommendation"))` by 1 November while SPY lost `r pct(-gb("^SPY"))`. Run on
any trading day from 17 August to 4 September it recommends a losing portfolio, and by
early September its list shares only `r min(sens$overlap_with_26aug)` of ten names with the
26 August one. The class average therefore reflects how teams implemented the picks more than the
model, and the lesson is that one two-month game cannot separate skill from luck.

## Why predicting returns is hard

Monthly stock returns are mostly noise: a forecast explaining one percent of their variance
would be worth a great deal. Whatever is predictable gets traded away once investors notice
it, and patterns estimated on 2022-2023 need not hold in 2025. Meanwhile a backtest has many
ways to look good by accident, and the class backtest found four:

1. It annualizes monthly returns with √252 instead of √12. The Sharpe ratio is
   `r num(orig$sharpe_correct, 1)`, not `r num(orig$sharpe_as_coded, 1)`.
2. An `ifelse()` slip gives every stock the top stock's weight, so weights sum to
   `r num(orig$mean_weight_sum)` on average: hidden leverage.
3. `recipe(target ~ .)` feeds in raw prices and volume. Yahoo adjusts past prices for later
   stock splits, so those levels carry information from the future.
4. Building the 20-day target drops the latest 20 days, so "current" picks use month-old
   signals.

## The improved model

The rebuilt model uses only stationary signals (12-1 and 6-1 month momentum, short-term
reversal, volatility, beta, distance from the 52-week high, relative volume), ranked across
stocks each month. It predicts returns relative to the month's average, uses one
non-overlapping observation per month from 2013, refits monthly on outcomes already known,
and takes its hyperparameters from 2019-2023 alone. It holds its top ten equally and pays
10 basis points per trade.

## Out-of-sample results

All models are scored on the same 34 monthly formations, January 2024 to October 2026, which
played no part in tuning. The simple benchmarks are holding all 95 stocks equally and a
one-line rule: buy the ten stocks with the best 12-1 month momentum.

### Predictive performance

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictive
#| tbl-cap: "Forecast quality, with forecasts and outcomes both measured relative to the month's average. Rank IC is the monthly rank correlation between forecasts and outcomes. R-squared compares squared errors with forecasting no difference between stocks."
ics |>
  transmute(Model = model,
            `Rank IC` = paste0(num(mean_ic, 3), " (t = ", num(ic_t), ")"),
            `R²` = ifelse(is.na(r2), "", pct(r2)),
            `Top 10 minus bottom 10, monthly` = paste0(pct(spread), " (t = ", num(spread_t), ")")) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

The class model ranks stocks well only with its price-level features. Without them its
rank correlation is indistinguishable from zero, and either way its forecasts are worse than
forecasting nothing (negative R²). The improved model's R² is positive but tiny, its top ten
beat its bottom ten by `r pct(ic("improved model")$spread)` a month with a t-statistic of
only `r num(ic("improved model")$spread_t)`, and its rank correlation is barely above the
momentum rule's.

### Investment performance

```{r}
#| label: tbl-invest
#| tbl-cap: "Portfolio results over the same 34 months, net of trading costs. Alpha is annualized against the 95 stocks held equally."
summ |>
  mutate(strategy = factor(strategy, c("class model", "improved model", "12-1 momentum, top 10",
                                       "equal-weight universe", "SPY"))) |>
  arrange(strategy) |>
  mutate(passive = strategy %in% c("equal-weight universe", "SPY")) |>
  transmute(Strategy = as.character(strategy),
            `Total return` = pct(cum_return, 0),
            Sharpe = num(sharpe),
            `Beta` = num(beta_spy),
            `Worst drawdown` = pct(max_drawdown, 0),
            `Alpha vs equal weight` = ifelse(passive, "", paste0(pct(alpha_ew), " (t = ", num(alpha_ew_t), ")")),
            Turnover = ifelse(passive, "", pct(avg_turnover, 0))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cum
#| fig-cap: "Growth of $1, net of trading costs, over the 34 out-of-sample months."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4
strat |>
  group_by(strategy) |> arrange(date) |> mutate(growth = cumprod(1 + net)) |> ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(date, growth, colour = strategy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("class model" = "#D55E00", "improved model" = "#0072B2",
                                 "12-1 momentum, top 10" = "#56B4E9",
                                 "equal-weight universe" = "grey35", "SPY" = "grey70"),
                      name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "growth of $1") +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

The improved model earns the most, `r pct(s("improved model")$cum_return, 0)`
(`r pct(min(seeds$cum_return), 0)` to `r pct(max(seeds$cum_return), 0)` across ten random
seeds), with under half the class model's turnover. But its beta is
`r num(s("improved model")$beta_spy)` and half its picks were chip stocks, 8 percent of the
universe: a concentrated bet on the technology rally, with twice the passive portfolio's
drawdown. Its Sharpe ratio is below simply holding the 95 stocks, its alpha is not
distinguishable from zero, and in the game window its picks lost
`r pct(-rd("game_improved.csv")$return)`, like the original's. The class model's alpha
disappears (t = 0.32) once the look-ahead features are removed. Neither offers returns an investor could rely
on.

## What the figures show together

@fig-game shows a fragile game result and a recommendation that lost money.
@tbl-predictive shows that, scored honestly, neither model forecasts much better than a
momentum sort, and @tbl-invest and @fig-cum show that the improved model's high return is
risk taken, not skill. The more sophisticated model still fails to predict returns; what
improved was the evaluation.

Scripts are in `R/`; details in `README.md`. Prices from Yahoo Finance via `tidyquant`.
